name: Showering twice daily

lead: Showering twice daily means washing in the morning and again later, often after exercise or before going out, to keep skin and hair clean and body odour controlled. It is a grooming baseline in appearance communities.
Washing removes sweat, oil and surface bacteria that contribute to odour. No published trial comparing twice-daily with once-daily showering was found in the sources consulted.

paras: People shower on waking, then again in the evening or after workouts, often followed by deodorant, moisturiser and fresh clothes.
No documented harms were found in the sources consulted; skin dryness is a concern some people raise.

angle.text: Appearance-focused users shower morning and evening, or after exercise, so sweat and surface bacteria are washed away and skin, hair and smell stay clean. The twice-daily frequency itself has not been studied.

lead: Showering twice daily is a hygiene routine, usually morning and evening or after exercise, adopted in appearance-focused communities to control body odour and keep skin and hair fresh. The look it aims at is clean skin without sweat or oil shine, tidy hair and no scent, which people count as part of overall presentation.[1][2]

Body odour comes mainly from bacteria acting on secretions of the skin's apocrine sweat glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits; Wikipedia says bathing daily with antibacterial soap reduces the bacteria that are the source of odour.[2] Deodorants reduce odour, and antiperspirants reduce sweating itself.[2]

Daily or multiple-times-daily bathing is described as common in Western cultures, with some people showering again after exercise or in hot weather.[3] No published trial comparing twice-daily showering with once-daily showering for appearance or odour was found.

paras: Regular bathing is an old practice; Roman civilisation is noted for it, and Han-dynasty officials were required to bathe every five days.[1] Showers developed from waterfalls and poured jugs to communal Greek and Roman showers; the first known mechanical shower was patented in England in 1767 and showers became common in private homes only in the 1970s.[3] Modern expectations differ between cultures and over time.[1]

Waterfalls were early natural showers, and ancient people later poured jugs of water over themselves. Greek communal shower rooms used lead-pipe systems, and Roman thermae spread across the Mediterranean [3]. The first known mechanical shower, hand-pumped, was patented in England by William Feetham in 1767, and the shower cabin was invented in 1839 [3].

French army barracks installed communal showers in the 1870s under the influence of François Merry Delabost, Prussia followed in 1879, a Vienna public bathhouse had a shower in 1887, and showers became common in private homes in the 1970s largely because of their cost [3]. Wikipedia says daily or multiple daily bathing is common in Western cultures and that modern cultures increasingly encourage a daily hygiene routine after 19th-century advances in science and medicine [3].

Skin bacteria such as Corynebacterium break down sweat lipids into smaller molecules that smell, and diet, sex, health and genetics also affect how a person smells.[2] Deodorants usually contain alcohol, antibacterial agents and perfume, while antiperspirants, including prescription aluminum chloride products, temporarily block sweat pores.[2]

Wikipedia states that bacteria on the skin, not sweat itself, cause most body odour. Apocrine glands, active from puberty and concentrated in the armpits, secrete compounds that skin flora convert into odorous molecules, and Staphylococcus hominis produces thioalcohol compounds that contribute to the smell [2]. Diet, the gut microbiome, sex, health and medication all affect odour [2].

Genetics matters too: the ABCC11 gene affects armpit odour, and its non-functional variant is common among East Asians but rare in European and African populations [2]. Wikipedia reports that eating more fruit and vegetables was associated with more pleasant-smelling sweat in one study, and that about 90 percent of Americans use an antiperspirant or deodorant [2]. For severe cases, doctors may prescribe aluminium chloride antiperspirants, and a surgery called endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy is an option that carries risks [2].

Proponents treat frequent showering as a baseline for grooming and scent, often alongside deodorant and fragrance. A T Nation member, discussing health habits in a thread on testosterone, mentioned twice-daily showers with special soaps as something he could do but did not bother with, which shows the routine is known as an optional step.[4] Some people also describe skin dryness as a concern with frequent washing; the reference pages consulted do not address this.

In an average home, showers are typically the third-largest water use after toilets and clothes washers. The average American shower used 17.2 US gallons over 8.2 minutes in a 2018 figure, the EPA says showering accounts for nearly 17 percent of residential indoor water use, and the US Department of Energy caps shower heads at 2.5 gallons per minute [3]. Two showers a day roughly double that use.

No studies found. No published trial comparing twice-daily with once-daily showering for odour or appearance was identified; Wikipedia's body odour article states that bathing daily with antibacterial soap reduces the skin bacteria that cause odour [2].
